=== 58777 SEIA Comments on Triennial Reliability Assessment Questions (as filed 3-2-26) .pdf ===
                                            PROJECT NO. 58777

    TRIENNIAL RELIABILITY                                §        PUBLIC UTILITY COMMISSION
    ASSESSMENT FOR THE ERCOT                             §
    REGION UNDER §25.508                                 §                       OF TEXAS

            COMMENTS OF SOLAR ENERGY INDUSTRIES ASSOCIATION ON
                            STAFF’S QUESTIONS

         COMES NOW Solar Energy Industries Association (SEIA) and files these comments1 in

response to the Commission Staff’s request for comment on questions filed in this project on

January 30, 2026. Staff requested comments be filed by March 2, 2026, so these comments are

timely filed.

         SEIA is the national trade association of the solar energy and storage industry and has

member companies engaged in the competitive Texas electricity market, as well as serving

residential, commercial, and industrial customers. Through advocacy and education, SEIA works

with its 1,200 member companies and other strategic partners to create jobs, champion the use of

cost-competitive solar in America, remove market barriers, and educate the public on the benefits

of solar energy.

                                      RESPONSES TO QUESTIONS

1) At the July 25, 2024 open meeting, the Commission approved setting the CONE at
   $140,000/MW-year for planning purposes in the ERCOT region, including the triennial
   reliability assessment. Based on stakeholder feedback, ERCOT has proposed a plan for
   updating this CONE value.
    a. Does CONE need to be updated for the 2026 reliability standard assessment? Why or
       why not?

         Yes, realistic and accurate model outputs are inherently dependent on realistic and accurate

model inputs, and technology options and costs are rapidly changing under today’s dynamic



1
     The comments contained in this filing represent the position of SEIA as an organization, but not necessarily the
     views of any individual member with respect to any issue.
 market conditions. Therefore, SEIA agrees that it is preferable to use the most accurate and updated

data available, including the cost of new entry (CONE), for ERCOT to perform its assessment.

SEIA further recommends including a sensitivity analysis for CONE values when considering

potential market design changes proposed as a result of the reliability assessment.

     b. If the Commission considers an updated CONE value, are the scope and list of tasks
        proposed by Brattle and Sargent & Lundy in ERCOT's January 15, 2026 filing an
        acceptable method to update the calculations? If not, please provide recommended
        modifications to their approach.

        ERCOT states in their Proposal to Update Cost of New Entry for the 2026 Reliability

Assessment, filed on January 15, 2026, that if approved by the Commission, an update to CONE

would include having the Brattle Group assess at least two gas-fired technologies (likely a small

frame combustion turbine (CT) and an aeroderivative CT). We note that projects being built

pursuant to the Texas Energy Fund (TEF) loan program could inform this analysis with actual costs

for thermal generation. Additionally, ERCOT states that the analysis could also include an

assessment of so-called “alternative” technology such as photovoltaic (PV) solar plus battery

energy storage hybrid system, if stakeholders and the Commission want to include this

technology.2 SEIA supports including an assessment of PV solar plus storage technology, as these

are not “alternative” technologies, but rather the technologies that developers are predominantly

seeking to build in ERCOT. As reflected in the Interconnection and Grid Analysis Update at the

ERCOT Board of Directors meeting on February 9, 2026,3 battery energy storage is currently

leading the ERCOT development queue, followed by solar, with natural gas and wind third and

fourth, respectively. Many of the solar projects have co-located battery projects, so a PV solar plus



2
    ERCOT Proposal to Update Cost of New Entry for the 2026 Reliability Assessment, (Jan. 15, 2026) at 2-3.
3
    See Item 9.2, Interconnection and Grid Analysis Update (Jeff Billo), ERCOT Board of Directors Meeting
    February 10, 2026, at Slide 5 (available at https://www.ercot.com/files/docs/2026/02/02/9.2-Interconnection-and-
    Grid-Analysis-Update.pdf).

                                                                                       SEIA Comments – Page 2
 battery energy storage hybrid system is a reasonable configuration to include in the CONE

analysis.

2) ERCOT has requested the Commission consider whether the load forecasts used in this
   study should align with the one that will be generated through the 2026 RTP compliance
   plan described in the Commission's rulemaking in Project No. 58480. ERCOT
   acknowledges that an updated load forecast that aligns with that compliance plan could
   be ready by April or May 2026, which would push back the timeline of the reliability
   assessment by at least a month.
   a. Should the Commission approve updating the load forecast used in the 2026 reliability
      assessment to align with the compliance plan being considered in Project No. 58480,
      even if it will delay work on the reliability assessment?

       Yes, as noted in our response to Question No. 1, realistic and accurate model outputs are

dependent on using realistic and accurate inputs. Therefore, SEIA supports using an updated load

forecast aligning with the 2026 RTP compliance plan, as proposed by ERCOT, given that ERCOT

also states that the delay in delivering the reliability assessment would be only a month. Prior load

forecasts have substantially overstated anticipated load growth by including speculative load

growth without considering aspects such as site control and financial commitment. We caution that

there have been substantial variances between ERCOT’s load forecasts and load that in reality is

interconnecting with the ERCOT system, so any and all forecasts, even an updated forecast

associated with the compliance plan, should be viewed with the appropriate amount of skepticism

during this period in which our electricity grid is rapidly transforming. Additionally, until load

participation in ERCOT markets is fully realized, it is likely that the grid operator will continue to

overestimate load growth impacts on the system, which will in turn skew the results of reliability

assessments toward unnecessary overbuild and related expenditures. ERCOT and the Commission

should proceed with caution.




                                                                            SEIA Comments – Page 3
    b. What other considerations should the Commission make regarding the load forecast
      used for the 2026 and 2029 simulation years?

       In addition to the above considerations, more analysis is needed to evaluate the likelihood

that any necessary transmission upgrades will be completed by 2029, and therefore the feasibility

that loads will be energized.

       SEIA also recommends that the 2029 load forecast include sensitivity analyses where there

are variables with considerable uncertainty, such as including sensitivities for higher and lower

load growth. Analysis should also include sensitivities around potential changes from 4CP

transmission cost allocation to alternative transmission cost allocation methodologies.

3) ERCOT proposed using the December 2025 Capacity, Demand, and Reserves (CDR)
   Report to create the base portfolio for evaluating the bulk power system in 2026 and 2029.
   This includes resource additions and retirements.
   a. Does the generation portfolio in the December 2025 CDR Report adequately capture
      the resource mix in both 2026 and 2029? If not, what additional assumptions should
      be made about resource additions and retirements?

       Projects being developed under the TEF represent the most current data, and to the extent

that the capacity of these projects differs from what is in the CDR, such information should be

incorporated into the analysis to ensure the most updated information. Projects that withdrew their

TEF applications but are still continuing to develop their projects should also be included.

4) Based on information provided by the transmission operators, ERCOT proposed using
   13,988 MW as the magnitude criterion of the reliability standard for the 2026 simulation
   year. For the 2029 simulation year, ERCOT proposes scaling the 2026 magnitude value
   by the ratio of the 75th percentile load forecast for 2029 to the 75th percentile load
   forecast for 2026, resulting in a magnitude value of 14,509 MW for the 2029 simulation
   year.
   a. Should the Commission use these values for the magnitude criterion in the 2026 and
       2029 simulation years? If not, what modifications to these values should be made?

       SEIA does not have an opinion on the specific number proposed for the study years 2026

and 2029. However, we do recommend that the Commission and ERCOT clarify that in calculating



                                                                           SEIA Comments – Page 4
 reliability metrics (frequency, duration, and magnitude), only the load shed for customers other

than large load customers with a demand of 75 MW or greater will be used. Large load curtailment

should not be considered load shed, as ERCOT has incorporated into its assumptions that these

large loads are generally curtailable.

5) ERCOT proposed using the EIA's 2025 Annual Energy Outlook and EIA Form 923 data
   to determine the natural gas and coal prices for the 2026 and 2029 simulation years. This
   results in prices of $2.84/MMBtu for natural gas and $2.47/MMBtu for coal in 2026 and
   $3.16/MMBtu for natural gas and $2.41/MMBtu for coal in 2029.
   a. Are these assumptions for fuel prices for the 2026/2029 simulation years reasonable?
       If not, what alternative sources of information should be considered to determine
       these fuels prices?

       These fuel price assumptions appear to be too low, which is problematic considering the

extent to which fuel prices drive market activity, including dispatch of demand-side resources and

battery energy storage resources. ERCOT should instead use the forward prices from a recent

market settlement date at a representative market trading hub.

   b. Should any sensitivity analyses on these fuel prices be considered?

       Yes, ERCOT should include fuel price sensitivities, given the extent to which fuel prices

affect market activities, including dispatch of demand-side resources and battery energy storage

resources.

6) For previous reliability assessments, ERCOT has treated all historical weather years as
   having equal probability. For this assessment, ERCOT proposed weighing recent years
   more heavily.
   a. Should the Commission consider not treating all historical weather years as having
      equal probability? If yes, do you agree with ERCOT' s proposed weighting of weather
      years?
   b. If you have an alternative weighting methodology, please provide additional details
      on your proposal. Please include justification for why your approach is better than
      what ERCOT has proposed.

       Weighing more recent weather more heavily than older weather years causes the impacts

of Winter Storm Uri to have more impact on the study results, although it is unclear whether this

                                                                         SEIA Comments – Page 5
 weighting is statistically justified. More work is needed to develop a framework that would

incorporate probabilistic methods to establish the appropriate weighting for extreme weather

events. Until that work is done, an alternative approach could be to compare the proposed

weighting methodology to additional alternative assessments, such as equally weighting the most

recent 15 years as well as equally weighting all 44 weather years.

7) ERCOT proposed using the multi-area reliability and economic dispatch modeling
   capability in SERVM to assess resource adequacy on a zonal basis that would account for
   transmission constraints between defined transmission zones. ERCOT states that any
   results from this analysis would be informational and not used to determine compliance
   with the reliability standard.
   a. Should the Commission approve an assessment of reliability metrics at the zonal level,
      understanding that these results would be purely informational and not used to
      determine compliance with the reliability standard?
   b. If so, do you have any proposed modifications to the approach ERCOT has
      recommended?

       SEIA has no comments on this issue at this time.

8) ERCOT proposed modifying how the model accounts for the effectiveness of the
   Commission's weatherization rule 16 TAC § 25.55. Previously, it was estimated to reduce
   weather-related outages by 85%, however under ERCOT' s proposed approach, the
   rule's effectiveness would decline during extreme temperatures
   a. Do you agree with ERCOT's recommendation to deviate from the 85% effectiveness
       for the weatherization rule?

       We support ERCOT’s recommendation as it includes performance gains from

weatherization but also captures risk during extreme cold conditions.

9) ERCOT has proposed assumptions for the outages:
   a. Are the assumptions for generation and ESR outage modeling reasonable? If not,
      what modifications do you propose?
   b. How should ERCOT treat planned transmission outages in the model?

       SEIA has no comments on this issue at this time.




                                                                        SEIA Comments – Page 6
 10) Please provide comments and recommendations on any of the model input assumptions
    that Staff has not specifically flagged in previous questions.

       SEIA has no comments on this issue at this time.

                                        CONCLUSION

       SEIA appreciates the opportunity to provide these Comments and looks forward to working

with the Commission and other interested parties on these issues.

                                            Respectfully submitted,

                                 EXECUTIVE SUMMARY

Q1:   SEIA agrees that it is preferable to use the most accurate and updated data available,
      including the cost of new entry (CONE), for ERCOT to perform its assessment. ERCOT
      should also include a sensitivity analysis.

      Projects being built pursuant to the Texas Energy Fund (TEF) program could inform this
      analysis with actual costs for thermal generation. SEIA supports including an assessment
      of PV solar plus storage technology.

Q2:   SEIA supports using an updated load forecast aligning with the 2026 RTP compliance plan
      given that ERCOT also states that the delay in delivering the reliability assessment would
      be only a month. Prior load forecasts have substantially overstated anticipated load growth
      by including speculative load growth without considering aspects such as site control and
      financial commitment. We recommend exercising caution with load forecasts.

      More analysis is needed to evaluate the likelihood that any necessary transmission
      upgrades will be completed by 2029, and therefore the feasibility that loads will be
      energized. SEIA also recommends that the 2029 load forecast include sensitivity analyses
      where there are variables with considerable uncertainty.

Q3:   Projects being developed under the TEF represent the most current data, and to the extent
      that the capacity of these projects differs from what is in the CDR, such information should
      be incorporated into the analysis to ensure the most updated information. Projects that
      withdrew their TEF applications but are still continuing to develop their projects should
      also be included.

Q4:   SEIA recommends that the Commission and ERCOT clarify that large load curtailment
      will not be considered load shed.

Q5:   These prices appear to be too low; ERCOT should instead use the forward prices from a
      recent market settlement date at a representative market trading hub.

      ERCOT should include fuel price sensitivities, given the extent to which fuel prices affect
      market activities, including dispatch of demand-side resources and battery energy storage
      resources.


                                                                         SEIA Comments – Page 8
 Q6:   Weighing more recent weather more heavily than older weather years causes the impacts
      of Winter Storm Uri to have more impact on the study results, although it is unclear whether
      this weighting is statistically justified. More work is needed to develop a framework that
      would incorporate probabilistic methods to establish the appropriate weighting for extreme
      weather events. Until that work is done, an alternative approach could be to compare the
      proposed weighting methodology to additional alternative assessments, such as equally
      weighting the most recent 15 years as well as equally weighting all 44 weather years.

Q7:   No comments.

Q8:   SEIA supports ERCOT’s recommendation as it includes performance gains from
      weatherization but also captures risk during extreme cold conditions

Q9:   No comments.

Q10: No comments.
